# Donald Knuth
Donald Knuth, a Midwestern Lutheran German computer scientist, was born in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and received his early education at Milwaukee Lutheran High School, where he demonstrated exceptional problem-solving skills. He earned a Bachelor of Science and a Master of Science in physics from the Case Institute of Technology in 1960 before receiving his PhD in mathematics from the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) in 1963. Knuth joined the Caltech faculty as an assistant professor but quickly shifted his focus to compiler development, notably creating an ALGOL compiler for the Burroughs B205. He later worked as a consultant for Burroughs Corporation and wrote the first volume of *The Art of Computer Programming* (1968), which became the foundation for his seminal multi-volume work on algorithms.
Knuth moved to Stanford University in 1969, where he became the Fletcher Jones Professor of Computer Science and later the Professor Emeritus of The Art of Computer Programming. At Stanford, he developed the literate programming methodology, embodied in the WEB system, which allowed source code to be both executable and readable documentation. He is perhaps best known for creating TeX, a high-quality typesetting system for mathematics and technical documents, and Metafont, a font definition language. Knuth's extensive bibliography includes works on algorithms, combinatorics, and recreational mathematics, and he was awarded the ACM Turing Award in 1974, the National Medal of Science, and the Kyoto Prize. His Chinese name, Gao Dena, was adopted in 1977 to facilitate recognition among computer programmers in China.
